abstract: Integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with Knowledge Graphs (KGs) results in complex systems with numerous hyperparameters that directly affect performance. While such systems are increasingly common in retrieval-augmented generation, the role of systematic hyperparameter optimization remains underexplored. In this paper, we study this problem in the context of Cognee, a modular framework for end-to-end KG construction and retrieval. Using three multi-hop QA benchmarks (HotPotQA, TwoWikiMultiHop, and MuSiQue) we optimize parameters related to chunking, graph construction, retrieval, and prompting. Each configuration is scored using established metrics (exact match, F1, and DeepEval’s LLM-based correctness metric). Our results demonstrate that meaningful gains can be achieved through targeted tuning. While the gains are consistent, they are not uniform, with performance varying across datasets and metrics. This variability highlights both the value of tuning and the limitations of standard evaluation measures. While demonstrating the immediate potential of hyperparameter tuning, we argue that future progress will depend not only on architectural advances but also on clearer frameworks for optimization and evaluation in complex, modular systems.

sections.body: The introduction motivates tuning for graph-enhanced retrieval-augmented generation. Standard pipelines are sensitive to chunk size, retriever type, top-k thresholds, and prompt templates, and graph-based variants add more interacting choices. The authors study this in Cognee, an open-source framework, on HotPotQA, TwoWikiMultiHop, and Musique. Each configuration is scored with exact match (EM), token-level F1, or DeepEval correctness, an LLM-based grader. The stated finding is that even modest parameter changes yield measurable improvements, and that metric choice and task characteristics strongly influence outcomes.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Hyperparameter tuning of graph-enhanced retrieval pipelines is underexamined, though many interacting settings affect multi-hop question answering.

sections.body: The section reviews retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), multi-hop question answering, knowledge graph question answering, GraphRAG, and hyperparameter optimization for RAG pipelines. It names Self-RAG and CRAG as recent refinements, and describes RoG as prompting language models to generate relation paths that graph traversal then grounds. For optimization, it cites Bayesian optimization under budget limits, context usage as a tunable variable, and reinforcement learning for full-pipeline tuning. It also notes multi-objective frameworks that trade off accuracy, latency, and safety.
sections.heading: Background and Related Work
sections.headline: Related work covers retrieval-augmented pipelines, three multi-hop benchmarks, graph-based question answering, and prior optimization of such pipelines.

sections.body: Cognee builds knowledge graphs from text, images, and audio through a default pipeline of ingestion, chunking, language model extraction, and indexing into graph, relational, and vector stores. Its retrieval layer supports vector search, graph queries, and hybrid methods. Its evaluation framework runs corpus construction, context-conditioned answering, comparison to gold references, and multi-metric grading on HotPotQA and TwoWikiMultiHop. The section argues that this modularity permits targeted tuning across ingestion, retrieval, and completion, and that the evaluation output gives quantitative feedback for an optimizer.
sections.heading: Automated Knowledge Graph Construction: Cognee
sections.headline: Cognee is an open-source framework whose modular pipeline and built-in evaluation let the whole system serve as an optimization objective.

sections.body: The authors built Dreamify, which treats the full Cognee pipeline as a parameterized process, with one configuration per trial. The six parameters are `chunk_size` (200–2000 tokens), `search_type` (text chunks or graph triplets), `top_k` (1 to 20), `qa_system_prompt` and `graph_prompt` (three variants each), and `task_getter_type` (with or without summaries). Grid search was judged impractical, and random search underperformed in early tests, so the optimizer is a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator. Scores are averages over questions between 0 and 1.
sections.heading: Hyperparameter Optimization Setup
sections.headline: Dreamify tunes six Cognee parameters with a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator, scoring each trial by a benchmark metric averaged over questions.

sections.body: Each experiment combines one benchmark (HotPotQA, TwoWikiMultiHop, or Musique) with one metric: exact match, F1, or DeepEval correctness. Instances were randomly sampled and then manually reviewed to remove ungrammatical, ambiguous, mislabeled, or unsupported examples, and this was done once before tuning. Each trial builds a single merged graph from the training passages and scores all training questions. Trials ran sequentially at about 30 minutes each. The best training configuration is reported on the test set, with bootstrap confidence intervals over QA pairs.
sections.heading: Experimental Setup
sections.headline: Nine experiments pair three datasets with three metrics, each running 50 trials on 24 training and 12 test instances per dataset.

sections.body: Table 2 reports baseline and optimized training scores, with the largest relative gain of 1496.0 percent on HotPotQA exact match. Table 3 shows hold-out results: HotPotQA correctness fell from 0.815 on training to 0.715, and most other metrics also dropped, while TwoWikiMultiHop F1 rose from 0.625 to 0.704. The authors attribute exact match and F1 penalties to phrasing differences, and report that the LLM grader gave several near-verbatim answers less than full credit. They note small hold-out sets, no early stopping or regularization, and that no single configuration was best on every benchmark.
sections.heading: Results and Discussion
sections.headline: Tuned settings beat baselines on all nine training metrics, but most hold-out scores fell below training scores.

sections.body: The conclusion states that systematic tuning of graph-based retrieval-augmented generation improved performance, with magnitude varying by metric and dataset. It says QA-based metrics do not fully capture the complexity of graph-based systems, and that generic tuning alone is unlikely to yield gains. Proposed future work includes alternative search algorithms, broader parameter spaces, multi-objective criteria, custom and domain-specific benchmarks, and a shared leaderboard for graph-augmented systems.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Tuning gave consistent but uneven gains, and the authors call for custom benchmarks and better evaluation of graph-based systems.

sections.body: The appendix describes Cognee's modular extract-cognify-load pipeline, in which the cognify stage applies schema-based transformations with Pydantic models to identify entities, relations, and attributes. Table 4 lists five default stages: ingestion, tagging, chunking, graph construction, and indexing. Table 5 lists six retriever types, including summary-based, chunk-level, graph neighborhood, RAG, graph completion, and graph-summary completion. The evaluation framework is a four-stage pipeline covering corpus construction, question answering, answer evaluation, and metric aggregation, configured through one declarative file.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix describes Cognee's extract-cognify-load architecture, its default pipeline stages, retriever types, and the evaluation framework.
